title: Horizons: Strategy
tagline: A foundations primer, then a full day on analysis before money is committed (Ch 1–3, 5)
audience: Business analysts, product owners, portfolio and strategy analysts, and BA leads who are asked to shape investment ideas before funding is approved — and who want an agile way to do it without writing a 60-page business case.
outcomes: Explain the agile mindset and the three planning horizons, and place any piece of your own work on the right horizon.
Frame a strategic problem without smuggling a solution into it.
Use outcome-focused analysis techniques (problem framing, value modelling, assumption mapping, real options) before money is committed.
Build a lean business case that states what evidence would prove the investment wrong.
Set up feedback loops that let a portfolio change its mind cheaply.
leaveWith: A lean business case that names what would prove it wrong
A horizon map of your own work

caseStudy.title: Delivered right first time: last-mile reliability
caseStudy.summary: Southern Cross Freight is a fictional national parcel and freight carrier moving around 38,000 consignments a day through 14 depots. Only 79% of consignments arrive within their promised delivery window, 9% fail at the first delivery attempt, and receivers and shippers chase status through the contact centre. The target outcome is on-time last-mile delivery of 92% or better within 12 months, with 'where is my consignment' calls down 40%. Throughout the day we take this one idea to an investment decision: a solution-free problem statement, tested assumptions and a lean business case.
caseStudy.disclaimer: Illustrative worked example using a fictional organisation.

modules.title: Welcome · foundations (Ch 1–3)
modules.subtitle: The agile mindset, the principles, and the three planning horizons in thirty minutes

participant.bigIdea: Agile analysis is not a smaller version of waterfall analysis — it is analysis sized to the decision in front of you.
participant.overview:
This opening block is a primer. Some of you have worked in agile teams for years; others have spent a career in stage-gated programmes. Either way, we need a shared language before we spend the day at the Strategy Horizon.

We cover three foundations quickly: the **agile mindset** (why we value learning over certainty), the **principles of agile business analysis** (the ideas that steer every technique you will use today), and the **planning horizons** model — Strategy, Initiative and Delivery — which describes how the *questions* an analyst asks change as the time frame shortens and the feedback gets faster.

The running case for the day is introduced here: *Delivered right first time* at Southern Cross Freight, a fictional parcel and freight carrier. Illustrative worked example using a fictional organisation.
objectives: Describe the agile mindset in your own words and contrast it with a predictive mindset.
Name the core principles of agile business analysis and give an example of each.
Explain the three planning horizons and what distinguishes them: outcomes, time frame and feedback cycle.
Place three pieces of your own current work on a horizon.

keyPoints.title: Mindset before method
keyPoints.body: Practices (stand-ups, backlogs, sprints) are visible; the mindset — expecting to be wrong, valuing fast feedback, putting customer value first — is what makes them work.

keyPoints.title: Principles steer techniques
keyPoints.body: Seeing the whole, thinking as a customer, analysing to determine what is valuable, getting real using examples, understanding what is doable, stimulating collaboration and continuous improvement, and avoiding waste.

keyPoints.title: Three horizons
keyPoints.body: Strategy (is this worth doing at all?), Initiative (what product or change will deliver it?), Delivery (what do we build next and how will we know it worked?).

keyPoints.title: Same analyst, different altitude
keyPoints.body: The horizons are not job titles. One BA often works across all three in the same week; the skill is knowing which question you are answering right now.

sections.heading: The agile mindset in one page
sections.body:
An agile mindset starts from a simple admission: **in complex work, we do not know enough at the start to plan the whole thing accurately.** Rather than fighting that uncertainty with bigger upfront documents, agile analysis reduces it in small, deliberate steps — by making assumptions explicit, testing the riskiest ones first, and adjusting the plan as evidence arrives.

For an analyst that changes three habits:

- **From completeness to sufficiency.** Analysis is "done" when it is enough to make the next decision well, not when every requirement is written down.
- **From sign-off to shared understanding.** The goal of a conversation is that the people who will make and use the solution understand it the same way — documents are a by-product.
- **From outputs to outcomes.** We measure success by the change in behaviour or results the customer sees, not by the number of features shipped.

sections.heading: The principles, practically
sections.body:
| Principle (paraphrased) | What it looks like on a Tuesday |
|---|---|
| See the whole | You ask *why* this initiative exists and what else in the organisation it touches before you analyse the detail. |
| Think as a customer | You describe the problem from the receiver's point of view, not from the depot system's. |
| Analyse to determine what is valuable | You rank options by value and evidence, not by who shouted loudest. |
| Get real using examples | You test a rule with three concrete consignments rather than debating it in the abstract. |
| Understand what is doable | You check constraints — transport regulation, WHS, data, capacity — early, so options are realistic. |
| Stimulate collaboration and continuous improvement | You make your thinking visible on a shared board and invite challenge. |
| Avoid waste | You stop analysing when the next decision is already clear. |

sections.heading: The three planning horizons
sections.body:
Think of the horizons as three zoom levels on the same landscape.

| | Strategy | Initiative | Delivery |
|---|---|---|---|
| Core question | Should we invest, and why? | What will we change or build to realise the strategy? | What is the next most valuable slice, and is it done? |
| Typical time frame | 1–5 years; reviewed quarterly | Months to a year; reviewed every few weeks | Days to weeks; reviewed every iteration |
| Feedback | Slow, lagging, business-level | Product metrics, customer response | Working software, demos, acceptance |
| Typical artefacts | Problem statement, lean case, value model | Product vision, impact map, feature roadmap | Stories, examples, acceptance criteria |

Today we work at the Strategy Horizon. If you later want to take the same thinking further, the standalone **Horizons: Initiative** and **Horizons: Delivery** courses each spend a full day on one of the other two horizons — optional, not prerequisites.

sections.heading: Meet the running case
sections.body:
Our illustrative case: Southern Cross Freight delivers only **79%** of consignments within the promised delivery window. Around 9% fail at the first attempt — nobody is home, the address is incomplete, or the item can't be left safely — and each failure adds two or three extra days plus a re-delivery cost. Receivers and shippers chase status through the contact centre. A strategic outcome has been proposed: **on-time last-mile delivery of 92% or better within 12 months, and 'where is my consignment' calls down 40%.**

At the Strategy Horizon our job is *not* to design a tracking app. It is to decide whether this is worth investing in, what we would need to believe for it to succeed, and how we would find out quickly if we are wrong.

*Illustrative worked example using a fictional organisation.*

activities.title: Horizon sort: your own work
activities.instructions: List three pieces of work currently on your plate. For each, write the question it is really trying to answer, then decide which horizon that question belongs to. Be honest — many people discover they are doing Delivery-level work on a Strategy-level question (or the reverse).

prompts.label: Work item 1 — the question it answers, and its horizon
prompts.placeholder: e.g. 'Member app requirements' → really asking 'should we build a member app?' → Strategy

prompts.label: One mismatch I noticed
prompts.placeholder: Where is the altitude of my work wrong for the decision?

participant.aiPrompt: You are helping a business analyst classify their work using the three agile planning horizons (Strategy: should we invest and why; Initiative: what product or change will realise the strategy; Delivery: what is the next valuable slice and is it done). I will paste a list of my current work items. For each one: (1) restate the underlying decision question in one sentence, (2) assign the horizon that question belongs to, (3) flag any item where the level of detail I am producing does not match the horizon, and (4) suggest the single most useful artefact for that horizon. Ask me one clarifying question if an item is ambiguous. My work items are:

quiz.q: Which statement best reflects the agile mindset for analysis?
opts: Analysis is complete when every requirement is documented
Analysis is sufficient when it supports the next decision well
Analysis is the responsibility of the product owner only
Analysis should be avoided in agile teams
quiz.why: Agile analysis is sized to the decision at hand; completeness for its own sake creates waste.

quiz.q: What primarily distinguishes the three planning horizons?
opts: The outcomes sought, the time frame and the speed of feedback
Whether the team uses Scrum or Kanban
quiz.why: Horizons differ by outcome, time frame and feedback cycle — not by role or tool.

quiz.q: 'Should we invest in improving last-mile delivery reliability at all?' is a question for which horizon?
opts: None — it is a governance question
quiz.why: Whether to invest, and why, is the defining Strategy Horizon question.

takeaways: The mindset — expecting to learn — matters more than any ceremony.
Principles are your tie-breaker when techniques conflict.
Every question you analyse lives on a horizon; match your detail to it.
Today we stay at Strategy: worth it, why, and how we would know we are wrong.

presenter.purpose: Build a shared vocabulary fast, set the 'you direct, the agent drafts' expectation, and introduce the running case so the day has a spine.
presenter.openingLine: "Before we talk about strategy, a quick confession test: hands up if you've ever written a detailed requirements document for something that was cancelled before anyone read it. Keep that memory — today is about not doing that again."

beats.label: Welcome, outcomes, logistics
beats.notes: Introduce yourself, the day's shape and today's three leave-with artefacts. Cameras-on norm, chat for parking-lot questions.

beats.label: Mindset and principles
beats.notes: Walk the principles table. Ask for one example from the room for 'get real using examples'.

beats.label: Three horizons
beats.notes: Show the comparison table. Stress: same analyst, different altitude.

beats.label: Running case and horizon sort
beats.notes: Introduce the case with the disclaimer. Run the horizon sort individually for 5 minutes, take two shares.

presenter.facilitationNotes:
Keep this tight — 30 minutes goes fast. Experienced agile practitioners may want to debate definitions; acknowledge and park. The purpose is shared language, not a lecture.

Read the disclaimer aloud the first time the Southern Cross Freight case appears, and again whenever a participant treats a figure as fact. Explain the AI pattern: participants bring the real inputs and judgement, the agent removes the blank page, and the BA reviews and owns the decision.
presenter.whatGood: Participants can name all three horizons and have at least one 'mismatch' noted from their own work.
presenter.commonFailure: Turning the foundations primer into a 30-minute agile 101 lecture — the fix is to stop at the horizon table and let the case carry the rest of the day.
debrief: Who found a piece of work at the wrong altitude?
Which principle do you most often break under pressure?
What would change if you sized analysis to the decision?
presenter.answerKey: **Horizon sort — model answers.** 'Write requirements for the new member app' at a professional sports club usually hides a Strategy question (*should we offer a digital membership channel at all?*) if funding is not yet approved. 'Update the claims-turnaround dashboard' at an insurer is typically Delivery. 'Agree the scope of the LMS upgrade programme' at a university is Initiative. A good mismatch note names the decision and the artefact that would actually serve it.
materials: Shared whiteboard with three horizon lanes

modules.title: The analyst at the Strategy Horizon
modules.subtitle: What the BA is for before an investment exists

participant.bigIdea: At the Strategy Horizon, the analyst's product is a better decision — not a better document.
participant.overview:
Most analysts arrive after the decision has been made. Strategy-horizon analysis moves you upstream, to where leaders are deciding which problems deserve investment. Here the analyst helps leaders see the whole system, frames the problem without a premature solution, tests whether the proposed outcome is realistic and measurable, and makes the assumptions behind the investment visible.

This session clarifies the role, the stakeholders you will work with and the kinds of contribution that earn you a seat in those conversations.
objectives: Describe the analyst's contribution at the Strategy Horizon.
Identify the stakeholders who own strategic decisions and what each needs from analysis.
Write a solution-free problem statement for the running case.
Distinguish a strategic outcome from an output.

keyPoints.title: Decision support
keyPoints.body: You help leaders choose between competing problems and options with explicit evidence and assumptions.

keyPoints.title: Problem before solution
keyPoints.body: Most strategic proposals arrive as a solution ('we need an app'). Your first job is to find the problem it is meant to solve.

keyPoints.title: Outcomes, not outputs
keyPoints.body: 'Launch a tracking app' is an output. 'Consignments arrive when promised' is an outcome. Strategies are judged on outcomes.

keyPoints.title: Seeing the whole
keyPoints.body: Map the value chain end to end — the delay is rarely where the loudest stakeholder thinks it is.

sections.heading: What the analyst does here
sections.body:
At this horizon you will typically:

1. **Clarify the strategic intent** — what goal or pain is driving this idea, and who owns it?
2. **Frame the problem** — describe the gap between today and the desired state without naming a solution.
3. **Size the value** — roughly, what is at stake if we solve it? Who benefits and how much?
4. **Surface assumptions** — what must be true for this investment to pay off?
5. **Outline options** — including 'do nothing' and 'do something small first'.
6. **Design the feedback** — what signals, at what intervals, would tell us to continue, pivot or stop?

Notice what is *not* on the list: detailed requirements, process models at task level, user stories. Those belong to later horizons and would be waste here.

sections.heading: Who you work with
sections.body:
| Stakeholder (illustrative) | What they need from you |
|---|---|
| Head of Depot and Last-Mile Operations | Confidence that the outcome is achievable and measurable without breaking operations |
| Chief Digital Officer | Clarity on whether a customer-channel investment is the right lever |
| CFO / portfolio board | A sized value case and a clear point at which to stop funding |
| Legal and Compliance | Early sight of constraints (for example Chain of Responsibility duties, WHS for drivers, privacy and SMS consent) |
| Subcontractor Fleet Manager | Understanding of impact on contract drivers' agreements, per-drop pay and KPIs |
| Key shipper accounts and receiver representatives | Assurance the change helps the people waiting for freight, not just the network |

sections.heading: Writing a solution-free problem statement
sections.body:
A good strategic problem statement has four parts: **who** is affected, **what** is happening, the **impact**, and the **evidence**. It deliberately avoids naming a solution.

**Weak:** *We need a new customer tracking app so receivers can see where their parcel is.*

**Strong:** *One in five consignments (21%) misses its promised delivery window, and around 9% fail at the first attempt. Receivers and shippers contact us repeatedly to check status, and every failed attempt adds two or three extra days and a re-delivery cost. We want to understand where the delay comes from and what it would take to deliver 92% of consignments on time.*

The strong version leaves room for many options: earlier booking data from shippers, address validation, asking receivers to confirm a window, better depot sort rules — or yes, an app.

sections.heading: Outcome versus output
sections.body:
A test you can apply to any strategic goal: *if we delivered this and nothing changed for the customer, would we call it a success?* If yes, it is an output.

- Output: *Deploy a tracking app by June.*
- Outcome: *On-time last-mile delivery rises from 79% to 92% or better.*
- Leading indicator: *Share of consignments booked with a validated address and receiver contact details.*

At Strategy you want one outcome everyone can repeat, plus two or three leading indicators that move sooner.

activities.title: Rewrite the brief
activities.instructions: The (illustrative) executive brief reads: *'Build a customer tracking app to modernise deliveries.'* Rewrite it as a solution-free problem statement using who / what / impact / evidence. Then write the strategic outcome and two leading indicators.

participant.aiPrompt: Act as a sceptical strategy reviewer. I will paste a problem statement for a proposed investment. Check it against four tests: (1) does it name who is affected, what is happening, the impact and the evidence; (2) does it smuggle in a solution or technology — if so, quote the phrase and suggest a neutral rewrite; (3) is the desired outcome measurable, with a baseline and target; (4) list at least four materially different solution options the statement still allows. Finish with a revised version of the statement under 90 words. My statement:

quiz.q: A health service wants to reduce outpatient waits. Which of these is a strategic outcome rather than an output?
opts: Median wait for a first specialist appointment falls to 30 days or less
Integrate the booking system with the EMR via middleware
quiz.why: Outcomes describe the change the customer experiences; the others are means to an end.

quiz.q: What is the main risk of a problem statement that names a solution?
opts: It narrows the options before the problem is understood
quiz.why: Naming the solution anchors everyone on one option and hides cheaper or better alternatives.

quiz.q: Which activity is usually waste at the Strategy Horizon?
quiz.why: Detailed stories belong to the Delivery Horizon; at Strategy the decision may still be 'don't invest'.

takeaways: Your product here is a better investment decision.
Strip the solution out of the problem before you analyse it.
Agree one outcome and a few leading indicators.
Know who owns the decision and what evidence they need.

presenter.purpose: Reposition the analyst as a decision-support partner upstream of funding, and produce the first leave-with artefact: a solution-free problem statement.
presenter.openingLine: "Most of us are invited in after someone has already decided what to build. This session is about what you do if you're invited in before."

beats.label: The role at this horizon
beats.notes: Walk the six contributions. Ask: which of these do you already do, even informally?

beats.label: Stakeholders
beats.notes: Use the table; ask participants to map the equivalent roles in their own organisation.

beats.label: Problem statements
beats.notes: Show weak vs strong. Highlight that the strong version still allows an app — we're not anti-solution, we're pro-options.

beats.label: Rewrite the brief activity
beats.notes: 15 minutes individually or in pairs, then 3 minutes of shares.

beats.label: Outcome vs output and close
beats.notes: Apply the 'nothing changed for the customer' test to two or three shares.

presenter.facilitationNotes:
Pairs work well for the rewrite — one writes, the other plays the executive who 'just wants an app'. Push for evidence in the statement; many first drafts omit it.

If a participant says 'my executives would never accept that', acknowledge the politics and suggest the framing: *we're protecting the investment by checking the problem first*.

roleplay.line: "The board has already said we're doing a tracking app. I just need you to write the requirements."
roleplay.curveball: "If you start questioning the app, you'll make me look indecisive."
roleplay.move: Agree with the intent, then reframe: 'Absolutely — let's make sure the app hits the 92% target. Can I spend two days confirming where the late deliveries actually come from, so the app is aimed at the biggest leak?'

presenter.whatGood: A problem statement with who / what / impact / evidence, no solution words, and a measurable outcome with a baseline.
presenter.commonFailure: Statements that swap 'app' for 'digital solution' and call it solution-free — the fix is to ask 'could a process change alone satisfy this statement?'
debrief: What solution words did you find hiding in your first draft?
Which stakeholder would push back hardest on a solution-free statement?
What evidence would you need to make the statement credible?
presenter.answerKey:
**Model problem statement:** One in five consignments (21%, illustrative) misses its promised delivery window, and around 9% fail at the first attempt. Receivers and shippers contact us repeatedly to check status, and each failed attempt adds two or three extra days and a re-delivery cost. We want to understand where the delay comes from and what it would take to deliver 92% of consignments on time.

**Outcome:** on-time last-mile delivery ≥92% within 12 months; 'where is my consignment' calls down 40%.

**Leading indicators:** % of consignments booked with a validated address and receiver contact; % of receivers confirming availability or a safe drop before route lock; first-attempt failure rate.

**Options still allowed:** receiver notification and confirmation; real-time booking from shippers; address validation; depot sort and route-planning rules; parcel-locker or collection-point options; a tracking app.

modules.title: Outcomes · time frame · feedback
modules.subtitle: What success looks like at Strategy, how long it takes to see, and how to learn sooner

participant.bigIdea: Strategic feedback is slow by nature — your job is to design faster signals that arrive before the money runs out.
participant.overview:
Each horizon is defined by three things: the outcomes it pursues, the time frame it operates over and the feedback cycle that tells you whether it is working. At Strategy, outcomes are business-level, time frames are long and true results lag. That combination is dangerous: an organisation can spend a year before finding out a strategy was wrong.

In this 90-minute block you will build an **outcome tree** for the running case, set realistic review intervals, and design a **feedback ladder** — leading indicators that move within weeks, linked to the lagging outcome that moves in months.
objectives: Describe the outcomes, time frame and feedback typical of the Strategy Horizon.
Build an outcome tree linking a strategic outcome to measurable drivers.
Distinguish leading and lagging indicators and choose credible ones.
Define continue / pivot / stop signals with review dates.

keyPoints.title: Outcomes are business-level
keyPoints.body: Customer, financial, regulatory or capability outcomes — expressed as a change from a baseline.

keyPoints.title: Time frames are long, reviews are not
keyPoints.body: A strategy may run for years, but it should be reviewed at least quarterly with real evidence.

keyPoints.title: Lagging results, leading signals
keyPoints.body: On-time delivery is lagging. Data completeness at booking is leading. You need both.

keyPoints.title: Decide your stop rule in advance
keyPoints.body: A stop signal written before funding is far easier to act on than one invented after sunk cost sets in.

sections.heading: Strategy-horizon outcomes
sections.body:
Strategic outcomes typically fall into four families: **customer** (faster, fairer, simpler), **financial** (cost, revenue, risk exposure), **compliance/regulatory** (meeting statutory obligations), and **capability** (what the organisation can do afterwards that it could not before).

For the running case:

| Family | Illustrative outcome |
|---|---|
| Customer | On-time last-mile delivery 79% → ≥92% |
| Customer/operational | 'Where is my consignment' calls down 40% |
| Financial | Value at stake ~$2.0m per year (illustrative), from fewer re-deliveries and calls and better shipper retention |
| Compliance | Safe-drop and re-delivery practices meet WHS and Chain of Responsibility duties |
| Capability | Ability to confirm receiver availability before routes are locked |

sections.heading: Building an outcome tree
sections.body:
An outcome tree breaks a strategic outcome into the drivers that cause it. Each branch should be something you can measure.

```
On-time last-mile delivery (lagging)
├── Data complete at booking
│   ├── % booked with validated address and receiver contact
│   └── Manifest lead time before depot cut-off
├── Time through the depot
│   ├── % sorted to the correct run on first scan
│   └── Median hours in depot
└── First-attempt success
    ├── % receivers confirming availability or safe drop before route lock
    └── First-attempt failure rate
```

The tree shows where to look. In the illustrative case, the biggest leak turns out not to be inside any one team: it is the failed first attempt being used as the *default way to discover* that a receiver isn't home — nobody asks them beforehand.

sections.heading: Time frame and review cadence
sections.body:
At this horizon you should be explicit about three dates:

- **Evidence date** — when the first leading indicator should move (e.g. 8–12 weeks after a pilot starts).
- **Review date** — when the portfolio will formally look at the evidence (quarterly is typical).
- **Outcome date** — when the lagging outcome should be reached (here, 12 months).

A strategy with only an outcome date is a bet with no exits.

sections.heading: The feedback ladder
sections.body:
| Rung | Signal | Speed | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Assumption tests | Days–weeks | Sample 50 recent failed attempts: what share were avoidable with receiver contact? |
| 2 | Leading indicators | Weeks | % of receivers confirming before route lock in the pilot depot |
| 3 | Operational results | 1–3 months | First-attempt failure rate |
| 4 | Strategic outcome | 6–12 months | On-time last-mile delivery |

Agree **continue / pivot / stop** thresholds on rungs 1–2. For example: *if fewer than 30% of sampled failures were avoidable with receiver contact, notification alone will not reach 92% — pivot to address and depot-process redesign*.

activities.title: Outcome tree for the case
activities.instructions: In small groups, build an outcome tree for 'on-time last-mile delivery ≥92%'. Aim for three levels. Mark each node L (leading) or G (lagging) and note whether you have a baseline.

prompts.label: Where I think the biggest leak is, and why

activities.title: Continue / pivot / stop
activities.instructions: Choose two leading indicators from your tree. For each, write a threshold and review date that would trigger continue, pivot or stop.

prompts.label: Indicator 1 — continue / pivot / stop thresholds and date
Indicator 2 — continue / pivot / stop thresholds and date

participant.aiPrompt: You are a performance-measurement analyst. Given the strategic outcome below, draft an outcome tree three levels deep. For every node give: a measurable definition, whether it is leading or lagging, a likely data source, and how quickly it would move after an intervention. Then propose two leading indicators with continue / pivot / stop thresholds and a review date. Flag any node where a baseline is unlikely to exist. Strategic outcome:

quiz.q: A university wants to lift first-year retention. Which is a leading indicator?
opts: First-year retention rate at year end
% of first-year students active in the LMS in week 2
Number of graduates in the year
quiz.why: Early engagement moves quickly and drives the lagging retention outcome.

quiz.q: Why set stop signals before funding?
opts: Because sunk cost makes it hard to define them later
Because agile teams don't need budgets
quiz.why: Once money is spent, people rationalise continuing; pre-agreed thresholds counter that bias.

quiz.q: In the illustrative case, the biggest leak was found to be…
opts: Slow sorting at the linehaul hub
The failed first attempt used as the default way to find out a receiver isn't home
quiz.why: A failed attempt had become the default discovery mechanism — a whole-system insight no single team owned.

takeaways: Every strategic outcome needs a baseline, a target and a date.
Build the outcome tree to find where to look.
Pair lagging outcomes with fast leading indicators.
Write continue / pivot / stop rules before money is spent.

presenter.purpose: Make the slow feedback of strategy tangible and give participants a tool (the feedback ladder) to speed it up.
presenter.openingLine: "If this strategy is wrong, how many months would it take us to find out? Let's make that number smaller."

beats.label: Outcomes at Strategy
beats.notes: Walk the four families with the case figures. Read the disclaimer.

beats.label: Outcome tree demo
beats.notes: Build the top two levels live on the whiteboard; reveal the 'default wait' insight.

beats.label: Group activity: outcome tree
beats.notes: Breakouts of 3–4. Visit each room at 10 minutes and check for measurable nodes.

beats.label: Time frame and feedback ladder
beats.notes: Teach evidence / review / outcome dates and the four rungs.

beats.label: Activity: continue / pivot / stop
beats.notes: Individual, then two shares.

beats.label: Debrief
beats.notes: Use debrief questions; capture good thresholds on the shared board.

presenter.facilitationNotes:
The outcome tree is where many groups stall. Prompt with 'what has to happen before a payment can be made?'. Encourage them to write unmeasurable nodes anyway and then fix them.

If time is short, cut the second activity to one indicator. Keep the debrief — it's where the 'decide stop rules in advance' message lands.
presenter.whatGood: Trees with measurable nodes, at least two leading indicators and thresholds tied to a date.
presenter.commonFailure: Thresholds like 'if it isn't working, stop' — the fix is to insist on a number, a data source and a date.
debrief: Which threshold would be hardest to act on politically?
What evidence date did you set, and could it be sooner?
presenter.answerKey:
**Model tree (level 2):** data complete at booking; time through the depot; first-attempt success. **Level 3 examples:** % booked with validated address and receiver contact (L); manifest lead time before cut-off (L); % sorted to correct run on first scan (L); median hours in depot (G/L); % receivers confirming before route lock (L); first-attempt failure rate (G/L).

**Model thresholds:** *% of failures avoidable with receiver contact in a 50-consignment sample by week 3 — ≥40% continue; 25–40% pivot to a narrower notification pilot (residential only); <25% stop and redirect to address and depot-process redesign.* *% complete at booking in pilot by week 10 — ≥70% continue; 50–70% pivot to assisted booking for key shippers; <50% stop and investigate.*

modules.title: Principles applied at this horizon
modules.subtitle: How each agile BA principle changes shape when the decision is an investment

participant.bigIdea: The principles do not change between horizons — what they ask of you does.
participant.overview: This shorter post-lunch block revisits the principles from the morning and applies each one specifically to Strategy-horizon work. The aim is a practical checklist you can bring into any investment conversation: a set of questions that, if you ask them, will make you useful in the room.
objectives: Apply each agile BA principle to a strategic decision.
Use a principles checklist to critique an investment proposal.
Identify which principle is most at risk in your organisation.

keyPoints.title: See the whole → system view
keyPoints.body: Map the end-to-end value stream across shippers, depots, subcontract drivers and receivers before choosing where to invest.

keyPoints.title: Think as a customer → worker's journey
keyPoints.body: Measure delay as the receiver experiences it, not by internal depot SLA.

keyPoints.title: Analyse value → compare options
keyPoints.body: Always include 'do nothing' and 'do something small' as options.

keyPoints.title: Avoid waste → stop early
keyPoints.body: Stop strategic analysis once the next funding decision is clear.

sections.heading: The principles at Strategy
sections.body:
| Principle | Question to ask at Strategy | Running case example |
|---|---|---|
| See the whole | Which parts of the system contribute to this outcome? | Shipper, linehaul, depot, subcontract driver, receiver |
| Think as a customer | What does the customer experience, end to end? | A missed window, a card in the letterbox and repeated status calls |
| Analyse to determine value | Which option produces the most value per dollar and per month? | Receiver confirmation vs tracking app vs parcel lockers |
| Get real using examples | Can we test the idea against real cases? | Walk five recent consignments through each option |
| Understand what is doable | What legal, data and capacity constraints apply? | WHS for safe drops; Chain of Responsibility; subcontractor agreements |
| Stimulate collaboration | Who must co-own this decision? | Depot Ops, CDO, subcontractors, key shippers |
| Avoid waste | What analysis can we skip for now? | Detailed app design until the receiver-confirmation hypothesis is tested |

sections.heading: Getting real at the Strategy Horizon
sections.body:
Examples are not just for user stories. At Strategy, *walk three to five real (or realistic) cases through the proposed change*. In the running case, take a standard residential parcel with a good address, a consignment from a shipper whose manifest arrives after the depot cut-off, and a bulky 30 kg item for an apartment that needs a two-person delivery. Ask: where does each spend its time today, and which option would change that?

This quickly shows that a tracking app alone barely helps the bulky apartment delivery, while confirming availability with the receiver before routes lock helps all three.

sections.heading: When principles conflict
sections.body: Principles sometimes pull against each other. *Avoid waste* says stop analysing; *see the whole* says you haven't looked at subcontract drivers yet. Resolve conflicts by asking **which decision is next and what it needs**. If the next decision is 'fund a 10-week discovery', you need just enough of the whole to scope that discovery — not a full end-to-end model.

activities.title: Principles critique
activities.instructions: Use the principles table as a checklist to critique the original (illustrative) proposal: 'Build a customer tracking app, $4m, 18 months'. For each principle, note one gap and one question you would ask.

prompts.label: Three questions I'd ask the sponsor
Principle most at risk in my organisation, and why

participant.aiPrompt: Act as an agile business analysis coach. I will paste an investment proposal. Critique it against these principles: see the whole, think as a customer, analyse to determine what is valuable, get real using examples, understand what is doable, stimulate collaboration and continuous improvement, avoid waste. For each principle give one gap you see and one question I should ask the sponsor. Then suggest three realistic example cases I could walk through the proposal to test it. Proposal:

quiz.q: At Strategy, 'get real using examples' most usefully means…
opts: Walking a few real cases through each option
quiz.why: Concrete cases expose which options actually change the outcome.

quiz.q: When 'avoid waste' and 'see the whole' conflict, you should…
opts: Do just enough to support the next decision
quiz.why: The next decision sets how much of the whole you need to see.

takeaways: Turn each principle into a question for the sponsor.
Use real cases to test options, even at Strategy.
Resolve principle conflicts by asking what the next decision needs.

presenter.purpose: Convert the principles into a practical critique checklist, and re-energise the room after lunch.
presenter.openingLine: "Here's a $4 million proposal. You have fifteen minutes and seven principles. Find the holes."

beats.label: Principles table walk-through
beats.notes: Move fast; ask for one example per principle from the room.

beats.label: Getting real with cases
beats.notes: Walk the three consignment types; show the app doesn't help the bulky apartment delivery.

beats.label: Principles critique activity
beats.notes: Pairs. Encourage blunt critique.

beats.label: Conflicts and debrief
beats.notes: Discuss conflicts; capture the 'principle most at risk' answers.

presenter.facilitationNotes: Post-lunch energy is low — keep people talking. Use chat waterfalls: everyone types their biggest gap and hits enter at the same time.
presenter.whatGood: Critiques that name concrete gaps (no do-nothing option, no worker view, no stop rule).
presenter.commonFailure: Generic critique ('needs more stakeholder engagement') — the fix is to demand which stakeholder and which question.
debrief: What was the most expensive gap you found?
Which principle is least practised where you work?
presenter.answerKey:
**Likely gaps:** no baseline or outcome target; solution-first framing; no options compared; subcontractors and shippers absent; no examples tested; WHS and transport obligations not checked; no stop rule; 18-month delivery with no interim learning.

**Strong sponsor questions:** What happens to on-time delivery if we do nothing for 12 months? Which of the 21% of late consignments does an app actually fix? What would we learn in the first 10 weeks?

modules.title: Analysis techniques
modules.subtitle: Value modelling, assumption mapping, options and real options for investment decisions

participant.bigIdea: Good strategic analysis makes the bet visible: what we believe, what it's worth, and what we'd lose if we're wrong.
participant.overview:
This is the technique-heavy block of the day. You will use four Strategy-horizon techniques on the running case: **value stream and value modelling**, **assumption mapping**, **options analysis** and **real options**. Together they produce the content of the lean business case you will finish in the final exercise.

Each technique is introduced briefly, demonstrated on the case and then practised.
objectives: Sketch a high-level value stream and locate the biggest delay.
Build a simple, transparent value model with ranges.
Map assumptions by importance and evidence, and pick the riskiest to test.
Compare options including 'do nothing', and use real options to keep choices open.

keyPoints.title: Value stream
keyPoints.body: Five to seven stages from trigger to outcome, with elapsed time on each. Not a process model.

keyPoints.title: Value model
keyPoints.body: A short chain from the outcome to dollars or other value, using ranges rather than false precision.

keyPoints.title: Assumption map
keyPoints.body: Plot assumptions by importance and by how much evidence you have. Test the important, unevidenced ones first.

keyPoints.title: Real options
keyPoints.body: Buy the right, not the obligation, to invest further — fund small, learn, then decide.

sections.heading: Value stream: where the days go
sections.body:
An illustrative strategic value stream for the case:

| Stage | Typical elapsed (illustrative) |
|---|---|
| Order placed → shipper books consignment | 0.5–1 day |
| Pickup and linehaul to destination depot | 1–2 days |
| Depot sort and route planning (routes lock 5 am) | 0.5 day |
| First delivery attempt | Day of promise |
| Failed attempt → card, re-delivery or depot collection | +2–3 days (9% of consignments) |

At this altitude you only need enough detail to find the biggest bar. Here it is the failed attempt — which suggests options around *asking the receiver before the route locks* rather than just faster trucks or sorting.

sections.heading: Value modelling with ranges
sections.body:
Keep it short and transparent. For example (all figures illustrative):

- Status calls avoided: 40% of ~X calls × handling cost → *$0.5–0.8m per year*
- Re-deliveries avoided through confirmed availability: share of failed attempts × average re-delivery cost → *$0.8–1.2m*
- Shipper retention from more reliable delivery → *$0.3–0.6m (low confidence)*
- **Total value at stake: roughly $1.6–2.6m per year; midpoint ~$2.0m.**

Show ranges and confidence. A three-year NPV around $2.9m with ~20-month payback (illustrative) is useful *only* if everyone can see the assumptions behind it.

sections.heading: Assumption mapping
sections.body:
List every belief the case depends on, then plot each on two axes: **importance** (if wrong, does the case collapse?) and **evidence** (do we know, or are we guessing?).

| Assumption | Importance | Evidence | Action |
|---|---|---|---|
| A meaningful share of failed attempts are avoidable if we contact the receiver first | High | Low | **Test first** — sample 50 failed attempts |
| We can contact receivers by SMS using shipper-supplied details within privacy and spam rules | High | Medium | Confirm with Legal |
| Subcontract drivers will adopt a common run-data feed | High | Low | Test with one subcontractor |
| Receivers will respond to a notification | Medium | Medium | Check response data from a similar carrier pilot |
| Status calls fall when receivers can see progress | Medium | High | Accept |

sections.heading: Options and real options
sections.body:
Always compare at least three options including **do nothing**:

| Option | Cost (illus.) | Time to first evidence | Addresses biggest leak? |
|---|---|---|---|
| A. Do nothing | $0 | — | No |
| B. Buy delivery-management platform, integrate with shipper and subcontractor systems via middleware, phased | $$ | 12 weeks (MVP) | Yes, with receiver confirmation |
| C. Custom tracking app, big-bang | $$$ | 12+ months | Partly |
| D. Process-only change: earlier manifest cut-offs + call-ahead rules for bulky items | $ | 6 weeks | Yes, partly |

A **real option** structures the investment so you can stop or expand cheaply: fund D now plus a 12-week MVP of B, with a decision point at week 12. The recommendation in the illustrative case is Option B, phased — receiver notification and real-time booking MVP first, then at-risk flagging and dynamic route optimisation.

activities.title: Assumption map
activities.instructions: List at least six assumptions behind the case. Plot them by importance and evidence. Choose the two to test first and design a cheap test for each (one to two weeks, minimal cost).

prompts.label: Top two to test, and why
Test design for assumption 1
prompts.placeholder: What we'll do, sample, signal, threshold

activities.title: Options with a real option
activities.instructions: Compare at least three options including 'do nothing'. Then describe a staged investment that buys a real option.

prompts.label: Options table (cost, time to evidence, addresses leak?)
My staged investment / real option
prompts.placeholder: Fund X now; decide Y at week N based on Z

participant.aiPrompt: You are a strategy analyst preparing an investment decision. Using the problem statement and context below: (1) sketch a 5–7 stage value stream with plausible elapsed times and identify the biggest delay; (2) list at least eight assumptions the investment depends on and rate each for importance and evidence (high/medium/low); (3) design a one-to-two-week test for the two riskiest; (4) compare four options including 'do nothing' on cost band, time to first evidence and whether they address the biggest delay; (5) propose a staged investment with an explicit decision point. Use ranges, not single figures, and mark any number you invented as an assumption. Context:

quiz.q: On an assumption map, which assumptions should you test first?
opts: The ones the sponsor likes most
quiz.why: These are the beliefs that could sink the case and that you currently cannot support.

quiz.q: Why use ranges in a strategic value model?
opts: They honestly show uncertainty and invite challenge
quiz.why: Single figures imply false precision; ranges show where more evidence is needed.

quiz.q: A 'real option' in investment analysis is…
opts: An option that is guaranteed to succeed
Funding a small step that preserves the right to invest further
An option chosen by the board
quiz.why: Real options buy learning and keep the choice to expand, change or stop.

quiz.q: Why include 'do nothing' as an option?
opts: It sets the baseline cost of the status quo
To make other options look better
quiz.why: Do nothing makes the cost of inaction explicit, which is often the strongest argument.

takeaways: Find the biggest bar in the value stream before choosing a solution.
Model value with ranges and show your assumptions.
Test high-importance, low-evidence assumptions first.
Stage the investment so you can stop cheaply.

presenter.purpose: Equip participants with four core Strategy-horizon techniques and generate the raw material for the lean business case.
presenter.openingLine: "Every business case is a bet. In the next ninety minutes we'll make the bet visible — what we believe, what it's worth, and how much we'd lose if we're wrong."

beats.label: Value stream
beats.notes: Draw the five stages; show the 10-day bar. Ask: what options does that suggest?

beats.label: Value model with ranges
beats.notes: Walk the illustrative ranges. Emphasise the disclaimer and the transparency of assumptions.

beats.label: Assumption mapping teach
beats.notes: Explain the two axes; place two assumptions live.

beats.label: Activity: assumption map
beats.notes: Breakouts. Push for tests that take under two weeks.

beats.label: Options and real options teach
beats.notes: Walk the options table; explain staging.

beats.label: Activity: options and real option
beats.notes: Individual or pairs.

beats.label: Debrief
beats.notes: Collect two staged investments; compare decision points.

presenter.facilitationNotes:
This is the densest block — protect activity time. If you're running late, shorten the value model teach rather than the assumption activity.

Watch for participants inventing precise numbers. Remind them: ranges and flagged assumptions, every time. If someone uses an AI agent to draft the value model, ask them to highlight every number the agent made up.
presenter.whatGood: Assumption maps with a clear 'test first' quadrant and tests under two weeks; a staged investment with a dated decision point.
presenter.commonFailure: Tests that are really mini-projects ('run a pilot for six months') — the fix is to ask 'what is the smallest thing that would change your mind?'
debrief: Which assumption would sink the case if wrong?
What's the cheapest test you designed?
Where is your decision point, and who makes the call?
presenter.answerKey:
**Riskiest assumptions:** share of failed attempts avoidable with receiver contact; permissibility of SMS contact using shipper-supplied details; subcontractor adoption of a common run-data feed.

**Model tests:** (1) Sample 50 failed attempts from last quarter; classify causes with Depot Ops — signal: % avoidable with receiver contact; threshold ≥40% continue. (2) One-hour session with Legal on privacy, consent and spam provisions — signal: yes/no plus conditions. (3) Ride along with one subcontract driver for two days using the proposed run-data fields — signal: % of drops with the data the driver needed.

**Model staged investment:** fund process change (earlier cut-offs + call-ahead for bulky items) and a 12-week receiver-notification MVP in one depot with one subcontractor; decision at week 12 on % complete at booking and first-attempt failure rate.

modules.title: Planning and delivery techniques
modules.subtitle: Lean business cases, portfolio flow and the strategy review cadence

participant.bigIdea: A lean business case is a hypothesis with a budget — and an exit.
participant.overview: Analysis is only useful if it shapes how money and attention flow. This session covers the planning techniques that connect Strategy-horizon analysis to the portfolio: the **lean business case**, **hypothesis-driven investment**, **portfolio Kanban** (limiting work in progress at the investment level) and the **strategy review cadence**.
objectives: Structure a one-page lean business case.
Express an investment as a testable hypothesis.
Explain how portfolio Kanban and WIP limits improve strategic flow.
Design a quarterly strategy review that uses evidence.

keyPoints.title: Lean business case
keyPoints.body: One page: problem, outcome, options, recommended first step, assumptions, cost of delay, what would prove it wrong.

keyPoints.title: Hypothesis framing
keyPoints.body: We believe [doing this] for [these people] will achieve [this outcome]. We'll know when [signal] by [date].

keyPoints.title: Portfolio WIP limits
keyPoints.body: Starting fewer strategic initiatives finishes more of them — and frees analysts to do them properly.

keyPoints.title: Cadenced review
keyPoints.body: Quarterly, with evidence from leading indicators; decisions are continue, pivot or stop.

sections.heading: The lean business case
sections.body:
| Section | What it contains |
|---|---|
| Problem | Solution-free statement with evidence |
| Outcome | Baseline → target → date |
| Hypothesis | We believe… we'll know when… |
| Options considered | Including do nothing |
| Recommended first step | The smallest investment that tests the riskiest assumption |
| Cost of delay | What each month of waiting costs (illus. ~$165k/month at $2.0m/yr) |
| Key assumptions | Top five with evidence rating |
| **What would prove us wrong** | Specific signals and thresholds that would stop or pivot |
| Review | Dates and decision-makers |

The last two rows are what most cases miss — and what make yours trustworthy.

sections.heading: Hypothesis-driven investment
sections.body:
Write the investment as a hypothesis:

> *We believe that real-time booking data plus receiver delivery-window confirmation will raise on-time last-mile delivery from 79% to ≥92%. We'll know we're on track when ≥70% of pilot consignments are complete at booking and the first-attempt failure rate falls below 5% by week 12.*

This keeps the conversation about evidence and gives the portfolio board an honest question to ask each quarter.

sections.heading: Portfolio flow and Kanban
sections.body:
Many organisations start far more strategic initiatives than they can staff. A **portfolio Kanban** board makes investment flow visible — *Funnel → Reviewing → Analysing → Ready → Implementing → Done* — with **WIP limits** on Analysing and Implementing.

For analysts this matters: WIP limits protect the time needed to do Strategy-horizon analysis properly, and the board makes it obvious when an idea has been 'analysing' for six months without a decision.

sections.heading: The strategy review
sections.body: A good quarterly review takes 60–90 minutes per portfolio and follows a fixed agenda: (1) outcome trend vs baseline; (2) leading indicators vs thresholds; (3) assumptions tested since last review; (4) decision — continue, pivot or stop; (5) next evidence date. The analyst prepares the evidence pack and facilitates, but the decision belongs to the accountable executive.

activities.title: Draft the hypothesis and cost of delay
activities.instructions: Write the investment hypothesis for the case, then estimate the cost of delay per month using the illustrative value at stake. Finally, place the initiative on a portfolio Kanban board and note what would move it to the next column.

prompts.label: Investment hypothesis
prompts.placeholder: We believe… for… will… We'll know when… by…

prompts.label: Cost of delay per month and reasoning
Current Kanban column and exit criteria

participant.aiPrompt: Turn my analysis into a one-page lean business case. Sections: problem (solution-free), outcome (baseline, target, date), hypothesis (we believe / we'll know when), options considered including do nothing, recommended first step, cost of delay per month, top five assumptions with evidence ratings, what would prove us wrong (specific signals and thresholds), and review dates. Keep it under 450 words, use ranges for figures, and list anything you had to assume at the end. My analysis notes:

quiz.q: Which section most distinguishes a lean business case from a traditional one?
quiz.why: Naming disconfirming evidence in advance makes the case testable and honest.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of WIP limits at the portfolio level?
opts: Initiatives finish faster and get proper analysis
quiz.why: Limiting work in progress improves flow and focus.

quiz.q: If value at stake is ~$2.0m/yr, the monthly cost of delay is roughly…
quiz.why: $2.0m ÷ 12 ≈ $167k — illustrative, and useful for urgency conversations.

takeaways: One page, with a hypothesis and an exit.
Cost of delay turns 'later' into a number.
Limit strategic WIP to protect analysis quality.
Review quarterly on evidence, and decide.

presenter.purpose: Connect analysis to investment flow and prepare participants to assemble their lean business case.
presenter.openingLine: "If your business case couldn't possibly be proven wrong, it isn't a business case — it's a wish."

beats.label: Lean business case anatomy
beats.notes: Walk the table; stress the last two rows.

beats.label: Hypothesis framing
beats.notes: Read the model hypothesis; ask what's missing in typical cases they've seen.

beats.label: Portfolio Kanban and review
beats.notes: Show a board; discuss WIP limits and the review agenda.

beats.label: Activity: hypothesis and cost of delay
beats.notes: Individual; share two hypotheses.

beats.label: Lead-in to final exercise
beats.notes: Explain the exercise and that they'll use their own investment idea.

presenter.facilitationNotes: Some participants will say their organisation insists on a 40-page template. Suggest the lean case as the cover page and decision tool, with the template as an appendix.
presenter.whatGood: A hypothesis with a measurable signal and date; a cost-of-delay estimate with reasoning shown.
presenter.commonFailure: Hypotheses with no signal ('we'll know when it works') — the fix is to require a number and a date.
debrief: What would your sponsor find most uncomfortable on this page?
Where would your initiative sit on the portfolio board today?
presenter.answerKey: **Model hypothesis** as in section 2. **Cost of delay:** ~$2.0m ÷ 12 ≈ $165k per month (illustrative), plus non-financial cost to receivers who wait in for deliveries that don't arrive. **Kanban:** likely 'Analysing'; exit criteria = riskiest assumption tested, lean case approved, first step funded.

modules.title: Exercise: apply to a live investment idea · close
modules.subtitle: Your own lean business case, and what happens after the investment decision

participant.bigIdea: Leave with a case that someone could say no to — that is what makes it worth saying yes to.
participant.overview: Apply today's techniques to a real investment idea from your own work (or continue with the running case if you have none). In 20 minutes you will assemble a lean business case that names what would prove it wrong, finalise your solution-free problem statement and update your horizon map. Then we close with a look at what happens once an investment is approved.
objectives: Assemble a lean business case for a live investment idea.
Finalise a solution-free problem statement.
Update your personal horizon map.

keyPoints.title: Use your own idea
keyPoints.body: The artefacts are more valuable when they're real. Sanitise sensitive details.

keyPoints.title: Direct the agent, own the judgement
keyPoints.body: Use the AI prompt to draft, then challenge every number and assumption.

keyPoints.title: After the decision
keyPoints.body: Once funded, the case becomes a product vision and an impact map at the Initiative Horizon.

sections.heading: Exercise brief
sections.body:
1. Choose a live investment idea (or use the running case).
2. Write the solution-free problem statement.
3. Complete the lean business case: outcome, hypothesis, options, first step, cost of delay, top assumptions, **what would prove us wrong**, review.
4. Update your horizon map from this morning: what will you do differently on Monday?

You may use your AI agent to draft from your notes. Review the draft as the BA: delete invented figures, sharpen the stop signals, and check that the problem statement is still solution-free.

sections.heading: After the investment decision
sections.body:
If the board approves Option B (phased), the question changes from *should we?* to *what exactly will we change or build, for whom, and in what order?* That is the Initiative Horizon, where the analyst builds a product vision, an impact map and an ordered set of features, each with a hypothesis and a signal.

**See also:** if you want to go deeper on that next step, the standalone **Horizons: Initiative** course spends a full day on it; **Horizons: Delivery** covers elaborating and verifying individual backlog items. Both are optional and self-contained.

activities.title: Lean business case for a live idea
activities.instructions: Complete each box. Aim for one page in total. Keep figures as ranges and mark assumptions.

prompts.label: Options incl. do nothing, and recommended first step
What would prove us wrong (signals + thresholds + dates)
Updated horizon map — one change for Monday

participant.aiPrompt: I am a business analyst finishing a lean business case. Using my notes below, draft a one-page case with: solution-free problem statement; outcome with baseline, target and date; hypothesis; at least three options including do nothing; recommended first step; cost of delay; top five assumptions with evidence ratings; 'what would prove us wrong' with specific signals, thresholds and dates; review cadence. Then critique your own draft: list any solution words in the problem statement, any invented figures, and any stop signal that is not measurable. My notes:

quiz.q: What makes a business case 'lean' in the agile sense?
opts: It is a testable hypothesis with a first step and explicit exit signals
It is written by the product owner
quiz.why: Brevity helps, but the defining feature is testability and staged commitment.

quiz.q: What changes when we move from the Strategy to the Initiative Horizon?
opts: The question moves from 'should we?' to 'what will we change or build, and in what order?'
quiz.why: The funded outcome carries forward; the question becomes how to realise it.

takeaways: You now have three artefacts: lean case, problem statement, horizon map.
The best cases name their own failure conditions.
Next, once funded: from investment to product.

presenter.purpose: Consolidate learning into the three leave-with artefacts and show where the work goes after an investment decision.
presenter.openingLine: "Last block. Bring a real investment idea — the messier the better — and let's make it something a board could say no to."

beats.label: Individual work
beats.notes: Circulate (or visit rooms); challenge stop signals.

beats.notes: Preview the Initiative Horizon; remind them to bring a funded initiative.

presenter.facilitationNotes:
Keep the clock visible. If people finish early, ask them to run the AI self-critique prompt on their case. End on time — it's 17:00.

Point anyone who wants to continue to the standalone Horizons: Initiative and Horizons: Delivery courses — optional, not required.
presenter.whatGood: Every participant has at least the problem statement and the 'what would prove us wrong' box completed.
presenter.commonFailure: Stop signals that are aspirations ('if stakeholders lose interest') — the fix is to tie each to a number and a date.
debrief: What's one thing you'll do differently in your next investment conversation?
What would prove your case wrong — and would you actually stop?
presenter.answerKey: **Model 'what would prove us wrong' (running case):** <40% of sampled failed attempts avoidable with receiver contact by week 3 → stop the notification-led approach; Legal advises SMS contact with shipper-supplied details is not permissible without consent → pivot to shipper-side opt-in at checkout; <50% complete at booking in pilot by week 10 → pause platform phase 2; first-attempt failure rate not below 6% by week 12 → return to board with revised options.
